entries.name: Bahay kubo
layout: one open room raised on posts
bamboo ladder to the door porch
no ceiling: hot air rises into the roof
blueprint: layer 1: . w w w .|w . . . w|w . . . w|w . . . w|. w d w .
layer 2: . r r r .|r r r r r|r r r r r|r r r r r|. r r r .
layer 3: . . r . .|. r r r .|r r r r r|. r r r .|. . r . .
legend: p stilt (haligi), w amakan wall, d door, r thatch roof, . open
entries.found: one to a few per lowland village, near rice paddies
entries.notes: The whole house can be lifted and carried by neighbours (bayanihan). Built to sway through typhoons; cheap to rebuild after a storm.

entries.name: Malay kampung house (rumah kampung)
layout: raised floor one room deep
front gallery for guests, main room and bedrooms behind
entries.found: kampung villages along rivers and coasts, Malaysia and Sumatra
entries.notes: Elevated against flood and snakes; the raised serambi is where guests sit and shoes come off.

entries.name: Thai stilt house (ruean thai)
layout: sleeping and living above the stilts
cooking done under the house or in a separate kitchen unit
multiple connected gables grow as the family grows
entries.found: flood plains and rice country, central and northeast Thailand
entries.notes: A cluster of linked gables marks a big household; the under-floor area stores rice and tools and shelters livestock.

entries.name: Dayak longhouse (rumah panjang)
layout: one long raised row of family rooms along a shared corridor and verandah
entries.found: riverbanks of the Borneo interior
entries.notes: Historic longhouses exceeded 100 m — a whole village under one roof. The verandah faces the river; each apartment is one family.

entries.name: Vietnamese stilt house (nhà sàn)
parts: open lower level for livestock and storage
layout: living above, animals and storage below
houses of a hamlet lined up on stilts
entries.found: mountainous north and central highlands of Vietnam
entries.notes: Living high, buffalo below; the gap between floor and roof sheds monsoon rain and ventilates in heat.

entries.name: Khmer stilt house
layout: single raised room, one door and a few windows
entries.found: rice paddy villages, especially around Tonlé Sap lake
entries.notes: The underside floods in monsoon; in the floating villages the same plan rides on bamboo rafts instead of stilts.

entries.name: Tongkonan
parts: saddleback roof with dramatically upswept gables (buffalo-horn profile)
carved frontage in red, black, yellow
layout: houses in a row facing north, granaries in a row opposite
3 vertical levels: attic for heirlooms, living room, under-floor for animals
entries.found: Tana Toraja villages, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
entries.notes: Not just shelter: the ancestral seat of a clan. Buffalo horns stacked on the gable mark status; most life happens outside the tiny dark interior.

entries.name: Rumah gadang
layout: matrilineal clan house: sleeping rooms flanking a long communal hall
entries.found: West Sumatra villages, one per extended clan
entries.notes: The iconic double-curved Minangkabau roof; raised on posts and built without nails so it flexes through earthquakes.

entries.name: Ifugao bale
parts: four huge corner posts on stone pyramid bases
notched ladder hauled up at night
layout: single tiny room raised rat-proof on four stones
entries.found: Ifugao rice terrace villages, northern Luzon, Philippines
entries.notes: Lives next to 2,000-year-old rice terraces; the stone-footed posts defeat rodents. Interior is a couple of square meters — daily life happens on the terraces.

entries.name: Bahay na bato
layout: service and storage below, family living above
upper floor lit by capiz windows, ventilated by ventanillas
entries.found: Spanish-colonial town centers, Philippines
entries.notes: The mestizo status symbol that evolved from the bahay kubo; still defines every old Philippine town and its earthquake-baroque look.

entries.name: Fale
parts: fale tele (great house) at village center
layout: open pavilion; woven mats define seating and rank
no walls: ceremony happens in full view
entries.found: Samoan and Tongan villages, one or two great fale per village
entries.notes: Built wall-less on purpose: the council meets and the chief presides in the open. The great fale anchors the village's matai system.

entries.name: Amazonian palafita (stilt house)
layout: raised one-room house over water or floodplain
floating deck linking neighbouring houses
entries.found: stilt villages on Amazon tributaries and várzea floodplains, Brazil and Peru
entries.notes: Houses ride floods that rise several meters a year; at high water every trip outside is by canoe.

entries.name: Maloca
parts: eastern door sacred, western door everyday
layout: elongated communal house; families along the sides, central plaza for ritual
entries.found: northwest Amazon (Colombia, Brazil, Peru)
entries.notes: One roof for a whole clan, 20 m or more long; the ridgepole embodies the line of descent. Neighbouring malocas share a ceremonial orientation.

entries.name: Tukul
layout: round single room, smoke escapes through the roof apex

layer 1: . w w w .|w w w w w|w w w w w|w w w w w|. w w w .

legend: w wall (stone or mud-brick), d door, r thatch, . open
entries.found: highland Ethiopia and Eritrea
entries.notes: The round thatched hut of the Ethiopian highlands; the very steep cone is insurance against heavy mountain rain.

entries.name: Kerala naalukettu (tharavadu)
parts: four blocks of rooms around an open courtyard (nadumuttam)
layout: courtyard in the centre, rooms on all four sides
kitchen north-east (the auspicious corner)
entries.found: ancestral homes across Kerala, India
entries.notes: Cooling by design: the open courtyard works as a chimney. Survives because laterite handles monsoon rain and termites.

entries.name: Bengali village hut (ghor)
layout: one or two rooms, porch at the front
entries.found: villages of the Bengal delta, India and Bangladesh
entries.notes: Rebuilt roughly every decade as thatch rots. The gabled 'bangla' profile travelled to Europe and became the bungalow.

entries.name: Rumah bolon
layout: open space below for livestock and storage; one big room above
entries.found: Batak Toba villages around Lake Toba, North Sumatra, Indonesia
entries.notes: Huge pitched gable with sculpted singa heads at each end; the under-floor shelters buffalo and the household sleeps above.

entries.name: Rumah joglo
layout: open pendhapa at the front for guests, enclosed living quarters behind
entries.found: Central and East Java, Indonesia; former aristocratic homes
entries.notes: The aristocratic Javanese house: the tumpang stacks rise tier upon tier above those four great pillars.

entries.name: Rumah limas
parts: great staircase to the front door
layout: floor rises in steps from front to back; each step marks rank
entries.found: Palembang, South Sumatra, Indonesia
entries.notes: Ceremony written in stairs — each terrace up is a higher grade of guest. The pyramidal limasan roof descends from Srivijaya.

entries.name: Balinese bale (compound pavilion)
parts: separate bale pavilions (bale daja, bale dangin, kitchen, granary)
layout: not one building: a fenced compound of small pavilions around a courtyard
one pavilion per function, open sides facing in
entries.found: Balinese villages, Indonesia
entries.notes: A Balinese 'house' is a walled village of miniature pavilions, not a single structure — modelling one box misses the point.

entries.name: Hale (Hawaiian grass house)
layout: single dark room; door kept low to keep the rain out
entries.found: restored Hawaiian homesteads and cultural sites, Hawaiʻi
entries.notes: Hale pili (pili-grass-thatched) housed pre-contact households; surviving examples are nearly all cultural reconstructions.

entries.name: Bure
parts: steep roof nearly to the ground
layout: single dark room; men's house (bure) separate from sleeping bure
entries.found: Fijian villages, Fiji
entries.notes: A solid dark volume whose roof almost sweeps the ground; modern Fijian villages often rebuild as timber frame with corrugated iron.

entries.name: Zulu beehive hut
parts: no wall/roof junction — one continuous shell
layout: round single room; doorway kept very low
entries.found: rural KwaZulu-Natal homesteads, South Africa
entries.notes: A woven beehive: sapling ribs bent into a dome and thatched; portable in pieces but usually rebuilt where the family settles.

entries.name: Rondavel
layout: round single room; homesteads circle a central kraal
entries.found: rural homesteads across Southern Africa
entries.notes: The ubiquitous round whitewashed rondavel with its perfect cone; adopted by settlers and now everywhere from farms to game lodges.

entries.name: Maasai manyatta
layout: ring of huts inside a thorn fence; cattle bedded down in the middle at night
entries.found: Maasailand, Kenya and Tanzania
entries.notes: The manyatta is the homestead, not a hut; the dung-plastered enkaji are women's work and the whole camp sleeps inside the thorn fence with the herds.

entries.name: Palhota
parts: thick thatch that runs nearly to the ground
layout: round or rectangular single room
entries.found: rural Mozambique and Angola
entries.notes: From Portuguese palha ('straw'); the generic word for African thatched dwelling on Portuguese-language maps.

entries.name: Palapa
layout: open-sided shelter for work and shade
entries.found: Yucatán, coastal Mexico, Belize; now at resorts worldwide
entries.notes: The open-sided shade roof descended from the Maya naj; modern resorts copied it onto every beach.

entries.name: Taíno bohío
layout: round family hut; framed with bent poles, thatched in cane
entries.found: archaeological sites and modern reconstructions, Greater Antilles
entries.notes: The Caribbean hut described by Columbus; the round bohío housed ordinary families while the rectangular caney held the chief.

entries.name: Shabono
parts: thatched roof ring with open centre
layout: oval ring of family shelters under one roof around an open plaza
entries.found: jungle clearings, southern Venezuela and northern Brazil
entries.notes: Temporary by design: a shabono is abandoned after 5–10 years when the gardens soil out or sickness strikes.

entries.name: Chattel house
parts: symmetrical façade with central door and flanking windows
two rooms, plus added sheds over time
layout: single or double room on unanchored footings
entries.found: Barbados and other West Indian islands
entries.notes: Portable by law and necessity: formerly enslaved landless workers needed a house that moved on an ox-cart. Moved in a day, reassembled the same day.

entries.name: Dai stilt house (ganlanfang)
layout: living above, animals and storage below
entries.found: Xishuangbanna, Yunnan, China
entries.notes: The Chinese 'ganlan house' of the Dai; the same stilt DNA as Thai and Lao houses across the border.

entries.name: Nhà rông (Central Highlands communal house)
layout: single great hall; village council sits inside
entries.found: Tây Nguyên villages, Vietnam
entries.notes: The communal roof dwarfs every dwelling around it; the village gathers, not sleeps, inside.

entries.name: Torogan
parts: panolong wing beams with naga carvings
layout: huge single square hall split by cloth dividers at night
no partitions by day; horse track crossing the front grounds
entries.found: Lanao del Sur, Mindanao, Philippines, near Lake Lanao
entries.notes: Royal ancestral house whose prow-shaped panolong beam ends make it look like a canoe resting on pillars; built entirely without nails.

entries.name: Mbaru niang
parts: seven-storey cone from base to peak (Ngaung, Tenda, Lobo, Lentar, Lempe Rae, Hekang Code)
lower floor for living and weaving, upper floors for food and seed
compang ancestor altar in the village plaza
layout: circular village of seven cones around a central altar
entries.found: Wae Rebo, Flores, Indonesia (1,100 m altitude)
entries.notes: UNESCO award-winning conservation icon; one cone shelters a whole clan across six storeys, roof sweeping to the ground.

entries.name: Musgum mud hut (tolek, cases obus)
layout: compound of tolek domes around a central courtyard
entries.found: Maga division, Far North Region, Cameroon and Chad
entries.notes: Shell-like tolek domes nearly 9 m tall built by mud coil-pottery technique; the relief grooves shed rain and give footholds for maintenance.

entries.name: Dogon toguna (palaver hut)
parts: carved wooden posts (often with fertility figures)
layout: rectangular open shelter; visitors must sit, nobody can stand
entries.found: center of Dogon villages, Bandiagara plateau, Mali
entries.notes: The great shelter: a ceiling so low it forces everyone to sit, engineered to keep heated council disputes from turning physical.

entries.name: Honai
parts: two internal levels (sleeping below, living above)
layout: men's honai and women's ebai as separate domes
pig wamai alongside; together a silimo cluster
entries.found: Baliem Valley and central highlands, Papua, Indonesia
entries.notes: It is cold at 1,600 m and above: honai are smoky snug domes keeping the hearth's warmth in, with no windows to leak it.

entries.name: Tonlé Sap floating house
parts: house on bamboo-raft foundation or tall stilts
fish pens under or beside the house
layout: floating street of houses, school and temple on rafts
villages migrate kilometres with the flood pulse
entries.found: Tonlé Sap Lake, Cambodia
entries.notes: Villages that commute with the seasons; in dry season the same houses stand on stilts several metres above bare lakebed.

entries.name: Taíno caney
layout: chief's rectangular house beside the batey ceremonial plaza
entries.found: archaeological sites, Greater Antilles
entries.notes: The rectangular counterpart to the round bohío; reserved for the cacique and for feasts and councils.
